products.title: Heritage One — Limited Edition, 50 Individually Numbered Pieces
products.body_html:
Some objects don't need a reference point. They don't arrive explaining themselves or borrowing credibility from something that came before. They simply exist with complete authority and leave you with the feeling that everything else was leading here.

The Heritage One is that kind of object.

 

 

Heritage

The Heritage line represents the highest expression of everything DRVN stands for.

Each model is a permanent design statement. Not a seasonal release. Not a colorway variation. A fully resolved object built around a single moment in automotive history that deserves to be remembered with more than a poster on a wall.

Every Heritage putter is individually numbered and engraved on the sole. Fifty pieces per model. When they are gone they are gone. There is no reissue. No second run.

Ownership is permanent. So is the number.

 

 

One

There is a certain kind of object that carries no asterisk. No qualifier. No footnote about what it was trying to be or what it was inspired by. It simply represents the furthest point anyone went in a particular direction and stopped because there was nowhere left to go.

The AMG One put a Formula One engine in a road car not because it was practical or sensible but because it was the most honest answer to the question of what was actually possible. No compromise dressed up as a feature. No limitation reframed as a choice. Just the absolute version of the thing.

The Heritage One arrives with that same energy. A classic blade profile executed without concession. Zero torque center shaft configuration for a stroke that works with the player rather than against them. And the most demanding insert in the DRVN lineup installed as standard, because this is not a putter that softens anything.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in torched Champagne Gold PVD, the One has a presence that feels earned rather than applied. Warm, deliberate, and completely unhurried. The kind of finish that looks like it has already stood the test of time before it ever left the workshop.

 

 

GT1-R — The Standard

Every other putter in the DRVN stable ships with the GT3 aluminum insert as its starting point. The Heritage One does not.

The One ships standard with the GT1-R. The most uncompromising insert in the lineup. Seventeen-four stainless steel, fully hardened, with no face milling of any kind. No grooves. No pattern. No surface geometry designed to manage or moderate what happens at impact. Just raw stainless meeting ball with nothing in between.

The result is a feedback experience unlike anything else in the stable. Every detail of the strike transmitted immediately and completely. The sound is sharper. The sensation is more direct. The communication between face and hands is total.

It is not for everyone. It was never intended to be.

 

 

Insert System

In motorsport the tire compound isn't an afterthought. It's one of the most consequential decisions made before a session begins. Same road, same car, same driver. Different compound, different character entirely.

The Heritage One operates on the same principle.

DRVN's interchangeable insert system allows the character of the putter to be tuned from the inside out. Material selection changes not just how the strike feels but how the head sounds, how it responds through the hands, and how it sits in terms of total mass. Aluminum inserts carry the head lighter and more fluid. Stainless inserts add weight, presence, and a more planted sensation through the stroke.

The putter doesn't change. Everything about how it responds does.

 

 

Inserts

GT3 — Standard A crisscross milled face that delivers balanced response and a slightly softened strike. Lively without sharpness. The starting point for most, and the permanent choice for many.

GT2 — Medium A pill-dash groove pattern that quiets the impact character. Smoother sensation, reduced acoustic presence, more controlled release. For players who prefer feel without commentary.

GT1 — Firm A fine-milled stainless face with a more defined strike and sharper audible response. Direct. Mechanical. The head speaking clearly through the hands.

GT1-R — Firm+ A raw, unmilled stainless face. No grooves, no surface interruption. Pure material meeting ball. Maximum communication, nothing filtered, nothing softened. Every detail of impact transmitted exactly as it happened.

 

 

 

Configuration

The One ships standard with the GT1-R stainless insert. The most direct, connected, and unfiltered configuration available in the DRVN lineup.

The classic blade profile and zero torque center shaft configuration work together to create a stroke that feels completely neutral and honest. No rotational pull. No head trying to open or close. Just the purest possible relationship between player, putter, and ball.

The One rewards players who have developed their stroke to the point where they want complete information rather than managed feedback. It does not compensate. It does not interpret. It simply tells the truth about every stroke, immediately and completely.

Aluminum insert configurations are available for players who want to explore a softer starting point. The architecture and zero torque geometry remain unchanged regardless of insert selection.

Neither is correct. Both are intentional.

There is a point that some players eventually reach where they stop looking for something more forgiving and start looking for something more honest. Where the goal stops being to protect the stroke and starts being to understand it completely.

Getting there takes time. The One was built for the player who already has.

Forty

In 1987 Enzo Ferrari ordered the creation of a car that would remind the world what Ferrari was actually capable of. No compromise. No concession to comfort or convention. A machine that existed purely to deliver the most visceral, connected driving experience the company could produce.

The F40 was the result. Twin turbocharged. Kevlar and carbon fiber body. A cockpit stripped to essentials. And that silhouette. Angular, aggressive, and so visually resolved that it has never stopped looking relevant.

The Heritage Forty pays homage to that machine through the details that made it immediately recognizable. The square cornered mallet profile draws from the hard edged geometry of the F40 body. The venting details across the top surface reference the iconic engine bay window and fender louvers that became defining features of the car. Every surface transition is deliberate, angular, and unapologetic in the same way the F40 always was.

Finished in Rosso Corsa. The red that carried Italian motorsport through its greatest era. The color that needs no explanation to anyone who has ever watched a Ferrari come through a corner at speed. On the Forty it carries the same weight it always has.

 

 

Insert System

In motorsport the tire compound isn't an afterthought. It's one of the most consequential decisions made before a session begins. Same road, same car, same driver. Different compound, different character entirely.

The Heritage Forty operates on the same principle.

DRVN's interchangeable insert system allows the character of the putter to be tuned from the inside out. Material selection changes not just how the strike feels but how the head sounds, how it responds through the hands, and how it sits in terms of total mass. Aluminum inserts carry the head lighter and more fluid. Stainless inserts add weight, presence, and a more planted sensation through the stroke.

The putter doesn't change. Everything about how it responds does.

Configuration

The Forty ships standard with the GT1 stainless insert. A deliberate starting point that suits the character of the head and the philosophy behind it.

The F40 was never a car that softened its responses. It told you exactly what it was doing at all times and expected you to keep up. The GT1 delivers the same philosophy through the face. Direct, mechanical, and immediately communicative. A starting point that matches the character of the object it lives in.

The center-shafted face-balanced configuration delivers a composed, controlled stroke with perimeter sole weighting that distributes mass to the extremities for stability and forgiveness without sacrificing the connected feel the Forty was designed to deliver. The result is a mallet that feels planted and authoritative at address and communicative through impact.

The Touring collection follows that same mindset. Restrained geometry. Balanced proportions. A design language centered around timelessness rather than theatre.

The Long Tail cars that emerged from that thinking became some of the most distinctive silhouettes in motorsport history. Not because anyone set out to make them beautiful. Because the physics demanded a shape and that shape turned out to be extraordinary.

The Touring LT was built in that spirit.

LT

The LT takes its name from the Long Tail racing cars of the late nineties. Extended rear bodywork, reduced drag, maximum stability at speed. A solution so aerodynamically pure it became its own design language.

That philosophy is visible throughout the LT from every angle. The swept rear profile extends further back than a conventional mallet, creating a head that feels planted and composed before the stroke even begins. The front to back sight line runs the full length of the head, bisecting the surface cleanly and providing a natural alignment reference that settles the eye without demanding attention. The aerodynamic surfacing flows without interruption from face to rear, rounded where it needs to move and deliberate where it needs to hold.

Underneath, the sole carries a detail that will be immediately familiar to anyone who has spent time around racing machinery. It needs no explanation.

Machined from 6061 aluminum and finished in hardcoat anodize, the LT has a presence that feels less like golf equipment and more like something that arrived from a different discipline entirely.

 

 

Zero Torque

The LT is engineered around a zero torque configuration.

In practical terms this means the shaft enters the head at a point precisely balanced with the center of mass, eliminating the rotational force that causes most putters to want to open or close through impact. The result is a stroke that stays on its intended path without the player compensating for a head that is fighting them.

It is not a gimmick. It is geometry. And for players who have spent years making unconscious corrections they were never aware of, the difference is immediate.

 

 

Insert System

In motorsport the tire compound isn't an afterthought. It's one of the most consequential decisions made before a session begins. Same road, same car, same driver. Different compound, different character entirely.

The Touring LT operates on the same principle.

Material selection changes not just how the strike feels but how the head sounds, how it responds through the hands, and how it sits in terms of total mass. Aluminum inserts carry the head lighter and more fluid. Stainless inserts add weight, presence, and a more planted sensation through the stroke.

The putter doesn't change. Everything about how it responds does.

GT1 — Firm A fine-milled stainless face with a more defined strike and sharper audible response. Direct. Mechanical. The head speaking clearly through the hands.

GT1-R — Firm+ A raw, unmilled stainless face. No grooves, no surface interruption. Pure material meeting ball. Maximum communication, nothing filtered, nothing softened. Every detail of impact transmitted exactly as it happened.

 

 

Configuration

The LT ships standard with the GT3 aluminum insert. A balanced starting point that suits most strokes and most conditions.

The LT is the most forgiving head in the DRVN lineup by design. The extended rear profile pushes mass further back and to the extremities, producing a moment of inertia that keeps the head stable through impact even when contact isn't perfect. Combined with the zero torque configuration, the result is a putter that removes more variables from the stroke than anything else in the stable.

Aluminum configurations keep the feel fluid and responsive. Stainless configurations deepen the planted quality the LT architecture already delivers, adding presence and feedback for players who want more communication without sacrificing stability.

The philosophy comes from an era of grand touring sports cars built not simply for performance, but for the experience of using them. Machines that felt rewarding on a winding road long after the trends around them had moved on.

The Touring collection follows that same mindset. Restrained geometry. Balanced proportions. A design language centered around timelessness rather than theatre.

 

 

Six Four

The Six Four takes its name and its character from one of the most recognizable sports car silhouettes ever produced: the Porsche 964.

For those unfamiliar, the 964 was the generation of 911 produced in the early nineties. Cleaner than what came before. More resolved. A car that retained everything essential about the air-cooled 911 while refining it into something more composed and enduring. It became a benchmark not because it chased trends but because it ignored them entirely.

That influence appears throughout the Six Four through proportion and surface treatment rather than direct imitation. The rounded rear shoulders reference the distinctive rear fender shape of the 964. The horizontal rear milling draws from the engine venting found across classic air-cooled 911s. Along the sole, a thin protruding section echoes the uninterrupted rear light bar that became one of the car's defining details. The recessed form at the center of the sole draws directly from the hood profile of the 964. Immediately familiar to anyone who knows the car.

Viewed from above the Six Four maintains a clean and restrained profile. Softened perimeter shaping and flowing transitions give it a more refined visual character than the harder-edged Mark One collection, while the center-shafted face-balanced configuration keeps alignment natural and the stroke composed from start to finish.

The result is a putter that feels less concerned with standing apart and more focused on delivering a balanced, deeply satisfying experience every time it is used.

 

 

Insert System

In motorsport the tire compound isn't an afterthought. It's one of the most consequential decisions made before a session begins. Same road, same car, same driver. Different compound, different character entirely.

The Touring Six Four operates on the same principle.

DRVN's interchangeable insert system allows the character of the putter to be tuned from the inside out. Material selection changes not just how the strike feels but how the head sounds, how it responds through the hands, and how it sits in terms of total mass. Aluminum inserts carry the head lighter and more fluid. Stainless inserts add weight, presence, and a more planted sensation through the stroke.

The putter doesn't change. Everything about how it responds does.

 

 

Inserts

GT3 — Standard A crisscross milled face that delivers balanced response and a slightly softened strike. Lively without sharpness. The starting point for most, and the permanent choice for many.

GT2 — Medium A pill-dash groove pattern that quiets the impact character. Smoother sensation, reduced acoustic presence, more controlled release. For players who prefer feel without commentary.

GT1 — Firm A fine-milled stainless face with a more defined strike and sharper audible response. Direct. Mechanical. The head speaking clearly through the hands.

GT1-R — Firm+ A raw, unmilled stainless face. No grooves, no surface interruption. Pure material meeting ball. Maximum communication, nothing filtered, nothing softened. Every detail of impact transmitted exactly as it happened.

 

 

Configuration

The Six Four ships standard with the GT3 aluminum insert. A balanced starting point that suits most strokes and most conditions.

The Six Four is built around stability and composure. The mid-mallet aluminum body and center-shafted face-balanced configuration distribute mass evenly, creating a stroke that feels unhurried and consistent. Moving through the insert range refines that character further without altering the fundamental nature of the head.

Aluminum configurations keep the feel fluid and responsive through release. Stainless configurations add a more deliberate, planted quality that suits players who want more presence and feedback without sacrificing the composed nature the Six Four delivers by design.

Neither is correct. Both are intentional.

products.title: MM-722 Ball Marker
products.body_html:
MM-722 Ball Marker

A piece of modern motorsport engineering, milled into stainless steel.

 

 

The MM-722 takes its form from the multi-spoke wheel carried by the SLR McLaren 722. A design that arrived at a specific moment in supercar history when the engineering ambitions of the early 2000s were starting to show up in every surface detail. Thin spokes, forward sweep, aggressive curvature. A wheel that looked like it was already moving before the car left the garage.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, the MM-722 carries that same sense of directed energy in a compact, precise form. The sweeping blades and clean outer rim translate naturally into stainless steel. The surfaces are crisp and the geometry holds the same sharp, purposeful attitude that made the 722's wheel one of the more recognizable shapes of its era.

The SLR McLaren 722 was named for Stirling Moss and his co-driver Denis Jenkinson's 1955 Mille Miglia victory. Seven hours, twenty-two minutes. The fastest road race ever run at that point in history. The 722 edition carried that number as a direct acknowledgment of what the car was built to represent. Performance with complete historical weight behind it.

The MM-722 brings that reference onto the course. A functional object used every round, carrying the character of a wheel design that arrived at exactly the right moment and has never stopped looking relevant.

products.title: Gated Shift Ball Marker
products.body_html:
A defining detail of analog performance, cut into stainless steel.

 

 

The Gated Shift takes its form from the exposed shift gate found in the great manual supercars of the late analog era. The layout is immediately familiar. Reverse offset, six forward gears, each position precisely defined within the gate. What was once a functional guide for deliberate mechanical movement translated here into a clean, machined surface.

There are sounds from that era that never fully leave. The mechanical click of a gear finding its slot. The short throw between ratios in a car that was built to be driven hard and rewarded you for knowing how. The gate wasn't just a guide. It was a conversation between the driver and the machine. Every shift a small confirmation that you were paying attention and the car was responding in kind. That kind of feedback disappeared when the paddles arrived and nothing has replaced it since.

Machined from 303 stainless steel with a fine linear brushed finish, the Gated Shift carries the same material honesty as the components that inspired it. The recessed pattern adds depth and subtle contrast without overcomplicating the design. Honest, mechanical, and built around the kind of tactile detail that defined an era before it disappeared entirely.

A simple object. But one that anyone who understood those cars will recognize the moment they pick it up.

Denser material, sharper acoustic response, and a more defined sensation at impact that leaves nothing ambiguous about what the stroke just did.

The angled groove pattern promotes early forward roll by reducing skid at the moment of contact. Not a softening of the experience. A sharpening of it. The face engages the ball cleanly and immediately, with a crispness that players who have spent time on faster greens will recognize and trust.

In motorsport terms the GT1 is the harder compound. More demanding, more communicative, and ultimately more rewarding for the player who has developed the stroke to use it properly. It doesn't interpret the strike. It reports it.

The geometry arrived at through decades of hands reaching for the same tool in the same situations, finding the same answer every time.

In any proper garage a good spanner becomes an extension of the person using it. It handles adjustments, setup changes, and the constant fine-tuning that separates a car that performs from one that merely runs. These tools accumulate marks and polish over time. Each one a quiet record of work done correctly, under pressure, without shortcuts.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, Spannerworks carries that same character. Dense, confident, and immediately familiar to anyone who has spent late nights dialing in a car with the right equipment in their hands. The defined edges give it a secure, natural grip. Parts made to be direct, tactile, and completely unambiguous about what they were for. The drilled pattern wasn't decorative. Those pedals lived in footwells of machines engineered for drivers who leaned in rather than backed off. Cars where every component was considered, every gram was accounted for, and the experience of operating them was the whole point. The hardware reflected that intent without needing to announce it.

The Piston Stroke takes its form from the piston and connecting rod of a V12. Scaled down, refined, and machined into a tool that carries the presence of a genuine engine component rather than a course accessory.

A V12 has a sound that stays with you long after the car has gone. Smooth at idle, climbing through the revs with a clarity that no other configuration quite replicates. That character comes from what happens inside the block. Pistons and connecting rods working through thousands of cycles per minute with complete mechanical honesty. The hardware is simple because it must be. Engineering reduced to its absolute essentials, where every gram and every surface exists for a reason.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, the Piston Stroke looks like something lifted from a pit garage after a long session, cleaned, and given a second purpose. The tapered rod profile sits naturally in the hand. The twin prongs carry the same precision as the components they reference. Nothing added. Nothing softened.

A tool that anyone who has spent time around serious engine work will recognize immediately.

products.title: Gated Six

The Gated Six takes its form from the aluminum shift knobs found in the great manual supercars of the nineties. Rounded, weighted, and sized for the hand rather than the eye. A form arrived at through function rather than styling, which is exactly why it felt so right and why it has never stopped looking correct.

A gated shifter had its own language. The lever moved through polished metal channels with a clean, deliberate note. You could feel the gearbox working through your palm. Each selection was physical, committed, and completely honest about what the car was doing underneath you. Anyone who spent time around performance cars of that period remembers the sound and the rhythm of it. The way a well-executed shift felt different from every other mechanical interaction in the car.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, the Gated Six carries the weight and clarity of a proper mechanical part. The six-speed shift pattern etched into the cap is the same layout that appeared in the magazines, on the posters, and in the cockpits of the cars that mattered most during that era. A single central prong. Nothing unnecessary. The whole tool shaped by the same philosophy as the object it references.

Twenty point eight kilometers of elevation change, blind corners, compression braking, and high speed surface variation that no other circuit on earth replicates. Manufacturers brought their prototypes there for one reason. The Nordschleife exposed everything. If a car survived it, the car was ready.

Lap times there became the language of serious automotive development. Drivers earned reputations by mastering it. Fans learned the corner names the way others learned capitals of countries. Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, The Ring carries the weight and feel of proper circuit hardware. Machined grip lines give it a confident, controlled feel in the hand. A functional tool built with the quiet seriousness of the place it references.

products.body_html:
A piece of air-cooled history, milled into stainless steel.

 

 

The P-64 takes its form from the Fuchs-style wheel carried by the Porsche 964. A design that became one of the most recognized wheel shapes in automotive history not because anyone tried to make it iconic, but because it was simply the right answer to the problem. Light, strong, and shaped entirely by the demands of real performance driving.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, the P-64 has the solid, confident feel of a small part pulled from a workshop shelf. The wide blades, open pockets, and crisp geometry translate naturally into stainless steel. Familiar immediately to anyone who spent time around air-cooled cars, early Porsche catalogues, or the wheel shapes that defined that generation.

There is a specific kind of person who grew up with a Porsche in the driveway or a poster of one on the wall and never fully got over it. The air-cooled era had a quality that nothing since has replicated. The sound coming over the hill before the car appeared. The way a 911 felt alive in a way that seemed almost unreasonable for something road legal. The Fuchs wheel was part of that identity for decades. Not because Porsche decided it should be. Because it was right and everyone knew it.

The P-64 brings that sensibility onto the course. A functional object used every round, carrying the character of one of the most enduring wheel designs ever produced.

products.title: VT-12 Ball Marker
products.body_html:
A compact piece of design taken from the analog supercar period, milled into stainless steel.

 

 

The VT-12 takes its form from the five-hole wheel pattern found on the great V12 supercars of the late analog era. A layout built around strength and structural honesty rather than visual effect. Solid material, clean geometry, and a form determined entirely by the forces it needed to manage.

Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, the VT-12 carries the weight and precision of something lifted from a period parts catalogue. The surfaces are crisp. The shape is immediate. The character is entirely mechanical.

Those cars lived in a specific part of memory. The sound before you saw them. The way a V12 at full cry felt like something that shouldn't exist on a public road. The posters that stayed on walls long after everything else changed. The wheel pattern was just one detail among many. But details are how you remember things. And this one has stayed recognizable for thirty years without anyone working to keep it that way.

The VT-12 brings that recognition onto the course. A functional object used every round, carrying the DNA of one of the most purposeful periods in automotive design history.

products.title: LM-40 Ball Marker
products.body_html:
A small piece of motorsport history, milled into stainless steel.

 

 

The LM-40 takes its form from the five-spoke wheel of the Ferrari F40. A design that became iconic not through decoration but through complete mechanical honesty. Light, direct, and purposeful in a way that made it immediately recognizable to anyone paying attention.

The marker follows the same philosophy. Machined from 303 stainless steel and finished in silver PVD, it carries the weight and surface quality of a precision-made part. Every spoke, every edge, every machined detail exists because it earned its place.

The F40 was the last Ferrari Enzo signed off on personally. That fact alone gives it a weight that no amount of horsepower or lap time could manufacture. For a generation of enthusiasts it wasn't just a car. It was proof that something could be built with total conviction and delivered without compromise. The wheel was part of that story. Five spokes. No excess. A design that looked exactly like what it was and nothing more.

The LM-40 brings that memory onto the course. A functional object used every round, built with the same seriousness as everything else in the DRVN stable.
